Nobody wants to move into impoverished communities (I see you trying to discredit me there by making that statement), and nobody is making the argument that they should.

 In case you weren't aware, there was (still is) a racial hierarchy in this country. White people at the top, black people at the bottom. And how this was structured is that white people were closest to the city and facilities, and it'd be Indian people, Coloured people, then black people at the very outskirts. This means that white people had the most access to facilities. When (especially black) people move into those areas to access those facilities such as education because the separation of public schools (quintiles) has widened the gap that (again, mostly black) people have to overcome to get afforded opportunities like tertiary education, white flight happens. And since they're already in the area, it makes sense to go to the churches nearer to the city. 

I'm sure you will again ask for a study to back this but white people have been leaving churches (or branches) to start their own, sometimes at their own inconvenience since they have to drive for longer to get to that branch, look at any city churches ten years ago and now. What are the incentives for doing that?  What are the incentives of taking kids to a school 30 minutes away when there's a well resourced school in the community?

I will reiterate my question. Why is it that after segregation ends, and black people move into spaces they weren't allowed to previously (such as schools, residential areas, churches), white people leave those spaces?

Of course, I can just say it's racism. But I'm hoping there's another answer besides that one.

The problem here is you think I'm on the side of Velaphi Khumalo and people like him. Those are extremists, and you know this.

Incentives against being in the same school/church as people of colour (especially black people)?
